title: The old plane trees
hook: at his country house Seneca finds the trees he planted grown old, and so is he

segments.voice: Yesterday: Cato, a good person kept before your eyes, and your line, stand a little straighter. Did your watcher come with you to one decision? Day four hundred forty-six.

Seneca goes out to his house in the country. The walls are cracking, and he scolds the man who manages the place: what are you spending the money on? The manager says, very politely, that it isn't his fault. The house is old. Seneca walks on, a little irritated, out to the plane trees by the path, and finds them bare and knotted. Has nobody been looking after these? The manager swears he's been digging and watering them. And then Seneca remembers who planted them. Today: the old plane trees.
screen: `A CRACKING COUNTRY HOUSE.` → `BARE, KNOTTED TREES.` → `THE OLD PLANE TREES.`

segments.voice: First, the house and the trees. Seneca opens letter twelve by saying that wherever he turns, he sees signs of his age. The house is crumbling, and he built it. The plane trees are gnarled, their branches twisted and dry, and he planted them himself and saw their first leaves. The manager has been digging and watering. The trees are simply old. So, Seneca realizes, is he. Second, the doorkeeper. Then at the door he sees a frail old man and asks, rather rudely, who on earth that is. The old man answers: don't you know me? I'm Felicio, the son of your old manager. You used to bring me little toys. I was your favorite. Seneca, who wrote this himself, lets the joke land on him. Everything he complains about, he's part of. Third, the turn. And then, instead of sinking, he turns. Let us welcome old age and love it, he says. It's full of pleasure if you know how to use it. Fruit tastes best just as the season ends. Youth is loveliest near its close. The last drink is the one the drinker savors. Every age has its own sweetness, and the late one has a kind all its own. Fourth, together. That's why today's line is we grew old together. Seneca and his trees, Seneca and Felicio, the house and the man who built it. Not a tragedy. A shared life. Something like that may be near you already: a tree in the yard, a friend from school, a mug, a jacket, a street.
screen: `THE HOUSE HE BUILT IS CRUMBLING.` · `FELICIO AT THE DOOR.` · `LOVE OLD AGE; IT HAS ITS SWEETNESS.` · `A SHARED LIFE, NOT A TRAGEDY.` · then, large: `WE GREW OLD TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Look around for something that has aged alongside you. A piece of furniture. A book with a cracked spine. A ring, a photograph, your own hands. If nothing is near, bring one to mind: a tree outside a childhood home, an old friend's face. Look at it carefully, the wear, the softness, the scratches. Notice what it has been through with you. And see whether something like fondness comes, the way it came for Seneca once he stopped scolding. The bell holds the time.
Platanus. Seneca's twelfth letter: the plane tree he planted himself, now gnarled with age, like the house and like him. Today's word.
Your line: we grew old together. Today, notice one thing or one person that has aged with you, and treat it with a little extra care. Day four hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: Readers of Seneca's twelfth letter often take it as an invitation to notice their own aging with humor and affection rather than complaint.

fork.setup: you're Seneca. you've just scolded your manager about the cracked walls and bare trees, and he says: they're old, sir. what do you do?
options: remember you built the house and planted the trees, and laugh at yourself.
fork.reveal: Seneca realizes the age is his own, and turns the moment into a lesson: love old age, it has its own sweetness.

original.note: Latin: the plane tree, broad and shady, the kind Seneca planted.

trapdoor: what you thought: a sad letter about getting old.
what it means: Seneca laughs at himself for blaming the house and trees for his own age, then says old age has its own sweetness.
what a scholar hears: the letter's humor is self-directed: Seneca, the owner of the whole estate, writes himself as the grumpy owner who gets the joke last.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: hook no longer has the manager say 'they're old, sir' about the trees (in 12.2 he swears he has dug and watered them); 'drives' and 'hasn't been in a while' removed; 'most of us' claim, told feeling in practice, Greek etymology and 'one of Rome's richest men' cut.

Letter 12.1–3: the suburban villa (suburbanum), the bailiff (vilicus), the crumbling building, the plane trees Seneca planted; Felicio, son of Philositus the bailiff, Seneca's 'deliciolum'. 12.4–5: 'complectamur illam et amemus'; fruit most welcome when going; boyhood's charm at its end; the last drink. Paraphrased; confirm details (e.g. 'little toys': Felicio says he was Seneca's pet; the sigillaria toys are Felicio's own detail).
'Just outside Rome' for the suburbanum: confirm.
